title: The P.A.

jokes.text: That sucked. I think I actually depressed Dolly Parton.
jokes.setup: Larry is coming off a late-night show taping and is seeking reassurance about his performance.
jokes.punchline: He claims to have depressed Dolly Parton — turning the expected post-show fishing-for-compliments into a moment of absurd self-laceration.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Larry Sanders opener: his vanity and insecurity fused into one line. 'Depressing Dolly Parton' is a vivid, specific image that earns a genuine laugh — Dolly is a beacon of positivity, so sapping her joy is a strong comedic bar. Very Larry to catastrophize immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, and those are big cups.

jokes.text: I quote, 'Honey, Larry is more fun than the cup ride at Dollywood.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just said he depressed Dolly Parton; Artie tries to reassure him by quoting her.
jokes.punchline: The Dollywood cup ride is an extremely modest compliment — being compared to a mild amusement park attraction is faint praise delivered as high praise.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Dollywood cup ride' is great comedy writing — it's low-key enough to be damning with faint praise while sounding like a genuine endorsement. Artie deadpanning this as comfort is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I feel like I have 20 pounds of wet sand in my head.

jokes.text: Yeah, and those are big cups.
jokes.setup: Artie has just quoted Dolly saying Larry is 'more fun than the cup ride at Dollywood.'
jokes.punchline: Larry's brain immediately fixates on validating the scale of the compliment rather than accepting it — he needs the cups to be big so the praise means more.
jokes.explanation: Five words that reveal Larry's entire psychology: he's not hearing the compliment, he's negotiating its value. The economy is exceptional — this is Larry Sanders distilled. One of the episode's better character-driven beats.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I was nuttier in the late eighties.

jokes.text: No, you were fresh, fast, focused, funny. Paula, tell our boy he's anything but sluggish. You are anything but sluggish.
jokes.setup: Larry is insisting he feels sluggish; Artie and Paula rush to disagree.
jokes.punchline: Paula robotically parrots Artie's exact instruction back as her 'honest' reassurance — exposing the entirely performative nature of the support staff's encouragement.
jokes.explanation: A deft bit of meta-comedy about yes-man culture in show business: Artie literally scripts Paula's reassurance in front of Larry, and she delivers it verbatim. The show-biz satire is clean and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: Hey, dad, where's the crapper? I gotta drop the kids off at the pool.

jokes.text: Triple espresso. Because I seem a little sluggish, don't I? No. No, not at all. Just drink it up. Oh, because I'm sluggish, I should... no, because if I had just done a long show, I'd want a triple espresso. Right. What do you mean long?
jokes.setup: Beverly brings Larry a triple espresso after he's been obsessing over feeling sluggish.
jokes.punchline: Larry interprets the triple espresso as confirmation he IS sluggish, then catches Beverly saying 'long show' and pivots to a new insecurity — the show's length — in a dizzying spiral of neurosis.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy: Larry's paranoia is so acute he cannot receive a cup of coffee without reading it as a diagnosis. The pivot to 'What do you mean LONG?' is a perfect escalation of his neurotic loop. Deeply Larry Sanders.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What a freak. What a big fucking freak.

jokes.text: Hey, did I tell you that I got a new television?
jokes.setup: Larry is spiraling about his sluggishness and the length of the show; Beverly is getting flustered trying to reassure him.
jokes.punchline: Larry abruptly changes the subject mid-anxiety spiral to announce a new television purchase — the comic beat is the whiplash non-sequitur, which Beverly and Artie presumably react to with bewilderment.
jokes.explanation: The abrupt pivot from existential dread to consumer enthusiasm is a classic Larry Sanders move — he's mercurial and self-absorbed enough that a new TV can break his own anxiety spiral. Solid character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Talk up. They're in the crapper, for God's sakes.

jokes.text: I feel like I have 20 pounds of wet sand in my head.
jokes.setup: Larry continues to complain about feeling sluggish despite reassurances.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of '20 pounds of wet sand' — not just sand, WET sand — is a delightfully precise hypochondriac image.
jokes.explanation: A strong piece of comic writing — the qualification 'wet' sand feels exactly like a hypochondriac's need to be precise about their misery. Quotable for its specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I was just thinking he's got such a great personality, maybe he should be the receptionist.

jokes.text: He never watches Letterman, never watches Leno, hates Nightline. That's flattering.
jokes.setup: Artie introduces his son Cully and says he's a big fan of the show.
jokes.punchline: Artie's evidence is entirely negative — Cully doesn't watch the competition — and Larry accepts 'that's flattering' with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry-insider comedy: being a 'fan' meaning only that you boycott competitors is a wry showbiz satire. Larry's earnest 'that's flattering' is perfect deadpan — he genuinely accepts negative-space loyalty as a compliment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You remember that summer we hired sheldon's son and we caught him in the xerox room with a copy of hustler? Remember what he was doing?

jokes.text: Where'd you get this stupid-looking peanut? Larry is the American Peanut Growers' Nut of the Year, 1989. I was nuttier in the late eighties.
jokes.setup: Cully notices an award on the wall that looks like a peanut and mocks it.
jokes.punchline: Artie defends it as a legitimate honor; Larry's response — 'I was nuttier in the late eighties' — is a perfectly timed self-deprecating non-defense that manages to be simultaneously defensive.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'I was nuttier in the late eighties' works on two levels — it's a wordplay pun on 'nut/nutty' and a genuine piece of Larry's self-mythology. The structure is flawless: insult → defense → self-subverting comeback. The pun is earned, not cheap, because it also reveals character.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What am I, a pussy? Why don't I send him something nice like a parasol and some earrings?

jokes.text: Hey, dad, where's the crapper? I gotta drop the kids off at the pool.
jokes.setup: Cully is being introduced to Larry and Beverly in a polite professional setting.
jokes.punchline: His request to use the bathroom, phrased in crude slang, is a jarring tonal mismatch with the formal introductions — immediately establishing him as a bull in a china shop.
jokes.explanation: 'Drop the kids off at the pool' is a well-known crude euphemism — not original, but the deployment in this formal introduction scene is well-timed and efficiently establishes Cully's character.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: If you're within an 8-foot radius, whoop it up.

jokes.text: What a freak. What a big fucking freak.
jokes.setup: Cully has just gone to the bathroom after the introduction; Larry presumably checks that he's out of earshot.
jokes.punchline: The moment Cully is gone, Larry immediately drops all pretense of hospitality and delivers his true verdict — viscerally and repetitively.
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the speed of the reversal — Larry is all fake warmth to Cully's face and instantly catty the moment he's gone. The repetition ('What a big fucking freak') escalates the sincerity of his disgust. Very Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Don't lip off to the head rooster, you're set.

jokes.text: Larry, that's the son. That's the one that got arrested. I can't hear you. That's the son, the one that... talk up. They're in the crapper, for God's sakes.
jokes.setup: Artie tries to quietly warn Larry about Cully's troubled past while Cully is in the bathroom.
jokes.punchline: Artie keeps whispering conspiratorially; Larry keeps yelling 'I can't hear you,' escalating the risk that Cully will overhear — culminating in 'They're in the crapper, for God's sakes' as if proximity to a toilet makes people deaf.
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe comedy of competing impulses: Artie wants discretion, Larry wants information, and together they're creating maximum exposure risk. The escalation of whisper-vs-yell is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: honestly, like some kind of cardboard shit.

jokes.text: He fell in with a bad crowd, just like his old man did.
jokes.setup: Artie is explaining Cully's troubled history — absent father, bad crowd.
jokes.punchline: He includes himself in the 'bad crowd' category without any self-pity or defensiveness — just matter-of-fact self-awareness that he was also a delinquent.
jokes.explanation: A quietly devastating piece of Artie characterization — his lack of self-pity and total absence of self-justification in admitting this makes it both funny and moving. The economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's the kissing disease. Don't kiss me!

jokes.text: We have to go through the J. Crew catalog. Oh, but Larry, I have to call the nutritionist. I mean, look at you. You're falling apart.
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to dodge Artie's favor request by saying he and Beverly have to review a catalog.
jokes.punchline: Beverly undercuts his escape plan by pivoting to her genuine concern about his nutritional health — 'Look at you, you're falling apart' — which is both a rebuke and an inadvertent endorsement of his earlier hypochondria.
jokes.explanation: A mild callback to the sluggishness spiral from the opener. Works as character texture more than a standalone joke — Beverly's blunt assessment is in character but the laugh is light.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I got fruit baskets comin' out of my ass.

jokes.text: I was just thinking he's got such a great personality, maybe he should be the receptionist.
jokes.setup: Artie asks Larry to hire Cully as a P.A.; Larry has already privately called him a 'freak.'
jokes.punchline: Larry suggests Cully be the receptionist instead — the job requiring maximum social interaction for a man he clearly finds repellent — as a passive-aggressive misdirection that sounds supportive.
jokes.explanation: Nice passive aggression from Larry — a subtly hostile suggestion dressed up as enthusiasm. The joke is in the subtext that he's either being genuinely clueless or intentionally sabotaging the idea.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: Dad, that network dipshit is sitting in your office waiting for you.

jokes.text: You remember that summer we hired Sheldon's son and we caught him in the Xerox room with a copy of Hustler? Remember what he was doing? Yeah, I know. I found him.
jokes.setup: Larry is expressing reservations about nepotism by invoking a past cautionary tale.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's 'I found him' — a quiet revelation that she personally discovered Sheldon's son mid-act — is the darker, funnier button delivered with total deadpan.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed two-beat joke. Larry thinks he's delivering the punchline ('remember what he was doing?') but Beverly's response reveals SHE is the actual punchline — she found him, making the trauma hers, not Larry's. The economy and structure are excellent. The 'Yeah, I know' from Larry before Beverly's line is a perfect misdirect.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: It's not as thrilling as un-jamming the xerox machine, but no, I do not mind.

jokes.text: What am I, a pussy? Why don't I send him something nice like a parasol and some earrings?
jokes.setup: Larry has just learned he sends Artie 'tulip explosions from Flowers by Drake' every birthday.
jokes.punchline: His self-laceration over the gift escalates into absurdly gendered insults about parasols and earrings — Larry's hypermasculine anxiety expressed through increasingly ridiculous hypothetical gifts.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Larry's toxic masculinity emerging from something as innocent as a flower arrangement. The escalation to 'parasol and some earrings' is funny in its specificity and absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: Hey, slim pants, yogurt?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: No, thanks, fat pants.

jokes.text: If you're within an 8-foot radius, whoop it up. That's the job? That's life.
jokes.setup: Artie is orienting Cully on his duties as a P.A. — keep the star happy.
jokes.punchline: 'That's the job?' / 'That's life.' — Artie reduces the entire entertainment industrial complex to mandatory sycophancy, delivered with Zen finality.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. 'That's life' as a response to 'That's the job?' is a perfectly compressed piece of showbiz philosophy — Artie's weary wisdom distilled into two syllables. This is what a great character line looks like: it's funny, it's true, it's uniquely Artie, and it lands in five words. Scores 8+ because it functions as both a great joke and a thesis statement for the entire series.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: Non-dairy is strawberry swirl, or as I like to call it, the queer's delight.

jokes.text: Don't lip off to the head rooster, you're set.
jokes.setup: Artie continues orienting Cully on how to survive working for Larry.
jokes.punchline: 'Head rooster' as the distillation of Larry's ego and temperament — the image of Larry as a barnyard alpha is both demeaning and accurate.
jokes.explanation: Artie's language is always vivid and old-school, and 'head rooster' is a perfect coinage for Larry. It implies strutting, pecking order, and fragile dominance in two words.

dialogue.line: I'll have that.
Lar will have queer's delight.

jokes.text: I gotta have lunch with the head rooster.
jokes.setup: Cully asks Artie to go to lunch; Artie can't.
jokes.punchline: Artie uses 'head rooster' again — this time as a callback to his own earlier line — but now it's used to blow off his own son to go coddle Larry. The irony of the callback landing here is pointed.
jokes.explanation: The callback earns its place: 'head rooster' was a piece of wisdom Artie shared with Cully, and he now uses it to explain why he can't have lunch with his son — demonstrating exactly the hierarchy Artie just described. Dark and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: I think he's very sexy, and I'd like to sleep with him.

jokes.text: Honestly, like some kind of cardboard shit.
jokes.setup: Cully tastes the nutritionist-approved lasagna Larry is being fed.
jokes.punchline: The pause before 'cardboard shit' — and the complete lack of diplomatic softening — establishes Cully as the only person in the building who will say what he actually thinks.
jokes.explanation: Works as character establishment — Cully's bluntness is funny in this environment of perpetual sycophancy — but the joke itself isn't original. The food-tastes-bad gag is familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: Good. I'm so tired of all the neurotic pussies around here.

jokes.text: Don't kiss me! Well, come here. Pucker up. Come on!
jokes.setup: Larry worries he might have mono (the 'kissing disease') and is telling people not to kiss him.
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately moves in to kiss him — either calling his bluff or genuinely amused by the hysteria — and Larry has to physically fend him off.
jokes.explanation: A nice physical beat between Artie and Larry — Artie's gleeful attempt to kiss a panicking Larry is in perfect character for both. Artie torments Larry with affection, which is one of their defining dynamics.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, maybe he went to 'this can't be yogurt.' Where's that? It's right near 'what is this, yogurt?' You know, I don't care if he goes to 'hey, that's my asshole.' I just want some yogurt.

jokes.text: I got fruit baskets comin' out of my ass.
jokes.setup: Hank asks Cully how it's going on his first day.
jokes.punchline: Cully's summary of the glamorous world of showbiz P.A. work is a crude, perfectly chosen image.
jokes.explanation: Cully's deadpan disillusionment with the glamour of showbiz, expressed through fruit basket logistics. Good character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Actually, I... I... I prefer it... extra-wet. It's, uh, more like real yogurt.

jokes.text: Dad, that network dipshit is sitting in your office waiting for you.
jokes.setup: Cully is relaying a professional message to Artie in front of others.
jokes.punchline: The clinical precision of 'network dipshit' — delivered as a neutral job description rather than an insult — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Works as both character comedy (Cully's utter lack of professional filter) and industry satire (everyone in the room knows exactly who 'the network dipshit' is). Efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Everyone screws up the yogurt. I used to screw it up back when it was ice cream, and my car smelled like rotten milk, but that's show biz.

jokes.text: Would you ask Dennis if they can give me a stairmaster? If not, I'll settle for a wheelchair, I swear to God.
jokes.setup: Larry hears there's a network executive waiting and immediately pivots to a personal equipment request.
jokes.punchline: His fallback position from 'stairmaster' to 'wheelchair' is a darkly funny escalation that reveals both his laziness and his hypochondria in one breath.
jokes.explanation: Larry's logic of 'I need to get in shape / I'd rather have a wheelchair' is perfectly calibrated lazy-hypochondriac comedy. The escalation from fitness equipment to disability accommodation is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: You get to wear shorts, drive around with the door open. It's perfect in this fucking heat.

jokes.text: Do I mind, Beverly? It's not as thrilling as un-jamming the Xerox machine, but no, I do not mind.
jokes.setup: Beverly asks Cully if he minds going out to get frozen yogurt — his first real errand as a P.A.
jokes.punchline: Cully's sarcastic reference to un-jamming the Xerox machine — a reference only the audience catches as a callback to the Sheldon's-son Xerox story — while simultaneously establishing his contempt for the errand.
jokes.explanation: A nice callback that works on two levels: as Cully expressing contempt for P.A. work, and as an echo of the Xerox room story — though Cully doesn't know that story, the audience does, which makes it a rewatch-bonus moment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I noticed that the armrest was missing and the seats were very, uh, sticky.

jokes.text: Blueberry, maple cream, pumpkin cheesecake, chocolate pudding, and chocolate nut fudge. How 'bout you, cutie pie? Yogurt?
jokes.setup: Cully is taking yogurt orders from the staff in an increasingly casual and flirtatious manner.
jokes.punchline: Calling Beverly 'cutie pie' on his first day, during his first real task, is a delightfully inappropriate escalation of casual confidence.
jokes.explanation: Mild character comedy — Cully's complete disregard for professional hierarchy is funny but this specific beat is underdeveloped. More setup than joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No one else has ever sat behind the wheel of my bentley except for the 3 previous owners and now... our cully.

jokes.text: Hey, slim pants, yogurt? No, thanks, fat pants.
jokes.setup: Cully takes yogurt orders from everyone; gets to Hank.
jokes.punchline: Hank's reflexive 'fat pants' comeback is perfectly balanced against 'slim pants' — it's a schoolyard insult duel that Hank gets dragged into with a 50-year-old's dignity.
jokes.explanation: Elegant in its economy — two words each way, the second perfectly mirroring the first. What makes it funny is that Hank gets sucked into Cully's register; Cully drags the co-host down to the level of a 12-year-old and Hank can't resist playing along. The body-image irony (Hank calling Cully slim pants and getting called fat pants back) is a light bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: Yeah, especially since I drove my shitbox into the bus shelter.

jokes.text: What is the non-dairy flavor? Non-dairy is strawberry swirl, or as I like to call it, the queer's delight. I'll have that.
jokes.setup: Cully is listing yogurt flavors; someone asks about non-dairy options.
jokes.punchline: Cully's impromptu renaming of strawberry swirl as 'the queer's delight' is gratuitously offensive — the joke is that he says it completely casually, and the room's discomfort is the comedy. Then Larry orders it anyway.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: Cully's casual homophobia establishes his rough edges; Larry's unflinching 'I'll have that' (ignoring the epithet entirely) is great deadpan; and the secondary beat of someone relaying 'Lar will have queer's delight' around the office compounds the absurdity. The slur dates the joke but it's deployed to reveal character, not to endorse.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That b-12 shot's doing no good whatsoever. Actually, maybe I should get a shot in each cheek, because one half of my ass feels like it's alive and rarin' to go and the other half feels depressed... and lonely.

jokes.text: Lar will have queer's delight.
jokes.setup: Cully coined 'queer's delight' for strawberry swirl; Larry ordered it.
jokes.punchline: Someone matter-of-factly relays the order using Cully's offensive nickname as if it's already standard terminology.
jokes.explanation: The callback's speed — it immediately follows — is what makes it work. Cully's slang has already been absorbed into the office vocabulary in about 30 seconds. The speed of institutional normalization is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Just look at kiefer sutherland.

jokes.text: That guy must be a moron. I think he's very sexy, and I'd like to sleep with him. Paula, he's a thug. Good. I'm so tired of all the neurotic pussies around here.
jokes.setup: Cully has apparently returned with wrong or no yogurt; people are complaining.
jokes.punchline: Paula's counter-take — finding him sexy BECAUSE he's a thug, then 'I'm so tired of all the neurotic pussies around here' — is the punchline, and it lands as both a critique of Cully and a devastating meta-comment on everyone else in the office.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. 'I'm so tired of all the neurotic pussies around here' is a perfectly economical piece of comedy writing — it's a character reveal for Paula, a devastating meta-commentary on the entire cast, and a perfectly timed subversion of Larry's complaint. The structure (setup complaint → expected agreement → total reversal) is textbook misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Tell him I'm uncomfortable around new people... that you don't like anyone who's younger than you, that you're still mad about that 'queer's delight' crack.

jokes.text: I don't want to be cruel, but how long does it take to get yogurt? Uh, Humphrey 'Yogart' is right around the corner.
jokes.setup: The yogurt still hasn't arrived; Larry is getting impatient.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Humphrey Yogart' — a pun on Humphrey Bogart — is delivered as an actual store name with complete deadpan, as if this has always been the name of the yogurt place.
jokes.explanation: A good pun, well-deployed. What elevates it: Artie uses it as a logical explanation ('that's why he's not back yet') rather than as a joke, maintaining his deadpan authority. The Bogart substitution is clean and unexpected.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: With me gone, he'll have you all to himself.

jokes.text: Well, maybe he went to 'This Can't Be Yogurt.' Where's that? It's right near 'What Is This, Yogurt?'
jokes.setup: Artie suggests Cully may be at 'Humphrey Yogart'; Larry and Artie escalate with increasingly absurd fake yogurt shop names.
jokes.punchline: The riff generates three escalating fake yogurt franchises — 'This Can't Be Yogurt,' 'What Is This, Yogurt?' — with Larry's genuine 'Where's that?' playing straight man.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best sequences. The fake yogurt shop names work as an escalating absurdist riff where each name describes a slightly worse quality of yogurt experience. 'This Can't Be Yogurt' and 'What Is This, Yogurt?' are riffs on real chains ('I Can't Believe It's Not Butter,' 'This Can't Be Yogurt' which is itself a real chain), but the absurdist escalation and Larry's straight-man 'Where's that?' give it real comedic structure. This reaches the 8 benchmark — it's a genuinely inventive piece of writing.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Why, because cully hasn't learned how to kiss ass yet like everybody else around here?

jokes.text: You know, I don't care if he goes to 'Hey, That's My Asshole.' I just want some yogurt.
jokes.setup: The fake yogurt shop name riff has been building; Larry needs to end it.
jokes.punchline: Larry caps the escalation with the most aggressively inappropriate fake store name imaginable, then pivots to sincere yearning for yogurt — the juxtaposition of obscenity and vulnerability.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. 'Hey, That's My Asshole' as a yogurt franchise name is an inspired escalation that works because it follows the logic of the naming riff while blowing past any reasonable endpoint. What makes it exceptional: the pivot back to sincere 'I just want some yogurt' — Larry's genuine need reasserting itself through the absurdity — is perfect comedy structure. This is Larry Sanders at its best: absurdist wordplay grounded in character neurosis. Easily the most quotable moment in the episode and a genuine piece of TV comedy writing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I just wanted my frozen yogurt frozen, that's all.

jokes.text: Larry, the boy has a bad attitude. Yeah, well, I don't think this is gonna work out.
jokes.setup: Artie has been defending Cully all episode; Larry has been passive-aggressively tolerating him.
jokes.punchline: The softness of 'bad attitude' from Artie (who has been watching Cully be genuinely offensive) is funny — and Larry's equally understated 'doesn't think this is gonna work out' is a masterpiece of conflict-avoidant corporate speak.
jokes.explanation: Good understated character comedy. Both characters are dancing around the obvious, and the gap between their diplomatic language and the reality of what Cully's been doing is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry King
dialogue.line: I can see this is a double Larry day.

jokes.text: Well, somebody should talk to Artie. Well, I'm rehearsing, so I can't talk to him. Oh, you're rehearsing. Yeah, I'm rehearsing a sketch.
jokes.setup: Beverly points out that someone needs to tell Artie his son isn't working out.
jokes.punchline: Larry's immediate retreat into 'I'm rehearsing' — delivered to Beverly while clearly not rehearsing — is his signature conflict avoidance in action. Beverly's straight-faced 'Oh, you're rehearsing' is the perfect deadpan acceptance of his lie.
jokes.explanation: Extremely on-brand Larry. His inability to confront anyone directly is the show's central engine, and this is a crisp instance — the excuse is transparently false, Beverly knows it's false, and neither of them addresses that.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: In the name of the sweet baby Jesus, why am I so fat?

jokes.text: I was going to tell you what a groovy new look that is for you. Yeah, thanks. Appreciate it. By the way, I gotta get my bong back.
jokes.setup: Beverly compliments someone on a 'groovy new look' in what seems like a normal workplace exchange.
jokes.punchline: Cully immediately follows up with 'I gotta get my bong back' — a completely unprofessional request that recontextualizes who he is and escalates the absurdity of his presence.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from professional pleasantry to bong retrieval is a sharp tonal gear-change. The casual delivery — as if reclaiming drug paraphernalia is a routine workplace request — is the source of the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: Really? Thanks for telling me, because I wouldn't know what a magazine is. I'm a moron.

jokes.text: It's gonna look nice in the garbage can.
jokes.setup: The melted yogurt has been handed to Hank; he initially seems grateful then realizes the state of it.
jokes.punchline: Hank's quiet verdict — that the melted yogurt is garbage-bound — is delivered with wounded dignity.
jokes.explanation: Hank's bruised aristocratic reaction to yogurt soup is a good Hank moment — he's offended not just by the quality but by the treatment.

dialogue.line: Look, I'm sorry that you're a 50-year-old p.a., but that's not really my fault.

jokes.text: Hank, that's Artie's son. (Beat.) Actually, I... I... I prefer it... extra-wet. It's, uh, more like real yogurt.
jokes.setup: Hank is complaining loudly about the melted yogurt; Larry has to inform him that Cully — Artie's son — is standing right there.
jokes.punchline: Hank's desperate, stumbling reversal — 'I prefer it extra-wet... more like real yogurt' — is the cringe comedy of someone trying to unsay something in real time and making it worse.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best cringe beat. The pause (implied by the transcript's structure) between 'Hank, that's Artie's son' and Hank's desperate reversal is where the comedy lives — we can see Hank computing the social damage and trying to undo it. 'It's more like real yogurt' as his saving-face logic is perfect: an objectively insane claim made with total commitment. Scores 8 because the structure is textbook — setup, reveal, cringe reversal — and the character specificity (only Hank would try this hard and fail this badly) is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Not after you stabbed the great one with a fork!

jokes.text: Son, I think you screwed up the yogurt, but that's all right. Everyone screws up the yogurt. I used to screw it up back when it was ice cream, and my car smelled like rotten milk.
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to make Cully feel better about the yogurt disaster.
jokes.punchline: Artie's reassurance takes the form of a historical analog — he too once destroyed temperature-sensitive desserts — grounding Cully's failure in a tradition of show-business incompetence.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully Artie moment. The logic that 'everyone screws up the yogurt, I did it with ice cream' is warmly absurd — he's normalizing failure through a very specific and oddly vivid personal history. 'My car smelled like rotten milk' as a show-business war story is the kind of detail that makes Artie Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: I was 6 years old. He was comin' at me.

jokes.text: That's all show business bullshit. What I'd really like to do is work for UPS.
jokes.setup: Artie is wrapping up his show-biz wisdom about screwing up the yogurt.
jokes.punchline: Cully dismisses the entire mythology of show business and announces his real ambition is UPS — a comic anti-climax that punctures all the industry glamour Artie just invoked.
jokes.explanation: A strong anti-glamour joke. The specificity of UPS — not 'a normal job' or 'something real' but the very specific package delivery company — makes it funny. It's also a clean piece of show-business satire: the most honest person in the building would rather be a UPS driver.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: Parr, gleason, cavett, and now Larry. It's always the same. Larry, a guy who's so limp, he's like a fucking sock.

jokes.text: You get to wear shorts, drive around with the door open. It's perfect in this fucking heat.
jokes.setup: Artie asks why UPS specifically; Cully elaborates.
jokes.punchline: Cully's entire career ambition reduces to 'shorts and an open door on a hot day' — a mundane, utterly practical desire that deflates any remaining pretense of showbiz aspiration.
jokes.explanation: Cully's specific UPS fantasy is beautifully mundane. The contrast between the Hollywood glamour he's surrounded by and his desire for ventilated work clothes is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Don't you dare call Larry a sock!

jokes.text: No one else has ever sat behind the wheel of my Bentley except for the 3 previous owners and now... our Cully.
jokes.setup: It emerges that Cully borrowed Artie's Bentley and left it with a missing armrest and sticky seats.
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'except for the 3 previous owners' undercuts his own claim of exclusivity with complete deadpan — he doesn't notice the absurdity of bragging about Bentley ownership while acknowledging it's a used car.
jokes.explanation: A very well-constructed piece of Artie deadpan. The self-undermining logic — 'nobody but the 3 people who owned it before me' — is funny because Artie says it with such gravity. The beat where he registers what he's said (if he does) would be gold on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Maybe he'll get that job at ups that he wanted.

jokes.text: Yeah, especially since I drove my shitbox into the bus shelter.
jokes.setup: Artie says they 'appreciate' Cully borrowing his Bentley, as if it was a privilege.
jokes.punchline: Cully's revelation that he crashed his own car into a bus shelter — thus necessitating the Bentley — is delivered with zero drama, as if this is a perfectly normal adult situation.
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'I drove my shitbox into the bus shelter' is the joke — Cully's complete lack of shame or apology about destroying his own car (and presumably the shelter) while borrowing a Bentley is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Cully
dialogue.line: I saw them my first day on the job. I saw the package. I said, 'let me take this to Larry personally.' I spaced. I left it in the trunk of the car.

jokes.text: What's wrong? My ass hurts. That B-12 shot's doing no good whatsoever. Actually, maybe I should get a shot in each cheek, because one half of my ass feels like it's alive and rarin' to go and the other half feels depressed... and lonely.
jokes.setup: Larry has just finished the show taping and is checking in with someone about his health.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'ass hurts' to 'one half is rarin' to go, the other half feels depressed and lonely' is a beautiful piece of hypochondriac absurdism — Larry's self-pity has migrated to his buttocks.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's top three jokes. The specificity of 'one half of my ass feels depressed... and lonely' is exceptional Larry Sanders writing — his neurotic self-analysis has been applied to his own gluteal region with complete sincerity. The ellipsis before 'and lonely' (inferred from pacing) suggests Shandling found the word in the moment, which is perfectly in character. This earns its 8+ because: it's original, structurally sound, could ONLY be Larry Sanders, and 'depressed and lonely ass' is genuinely novel absurdist comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Isn't tampering with the mail a felony?

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, he's Artie's son.

jokes.text: Producer's kid or something? Yeah, that's the producer's son. He's a good boy. Good-looking boy.
jokes.setup: After Cully has bothered Chris Isaak for 20 minutes, someone explains who he is.
jokes.punchline: The repetition of 'good boy, good-looking boy' — the same words Artie and Larry have been using all episode to smooth over Cully's transgressions — has become a running coda.
jokes.explanation: The 'good-looking boy' phrase has become a running gag of protective euphemism — each time it appears, it's covering for something worse. Works as a running gag callback.

jokes.text: The doctor stuck a needle in the fleshy part of my ass. That's how it was.
jokes.setup: Someone asks how the B-12 shot went.
jokes.punchline: 'That's how it was' — Larry's solemn coda to the medical description, delivered like a war veteran recounting a battle.
jokes.explanation: 'That's how it was' as a summary of 'needle in my ass' is a great piece of understatement — Larry's gravity about minor medical procedures is perfectly captured. The gravity sells it.

jokes.text: I should never have hired Cully to work here. He fucked up Hank's car, he had Chris Isaak on the phone for 20 minutes. He's rude to everyone except Paula.
jokes.setup: Larry is reviewing Cully's first day.
jokes.punchline: 'He's rude to everyone except Paula' — the implicit exception is funnier than the charges, because Paula LIKED that he was a thug.
jokes.explanation: Good callback — 'except Paula' lands because we know WHY Paula likes Cully (she finds his thuggishness appealing). The callback rewards attention.

jokes.text: Nepotism is always bad. Just look at Kiefer Sutherland.
jokes.setup: Larry says nepotism is a bad idea; Artie offers evidence.
jokes.punchline: Kiefer Sutherland — Donald Sutherland's son — as the cautionary example of showbiz nepotism is a sharp, specific industry joke. (The joke implies Kiefer isn't good, which is itself debatable, making it funnier.)
jokes.explanation: Sharp four-word industry-insider joke. The specificity of 'Kiefer Sutherland' over a generic example gives it bite. The ambiguity (is Kiefer bad because of nepotism, or despite it?) adds a layer. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Tell him I'm uncomfortable around new people. Yeah, tell him that, uh... that you're uncomfortable around new people... that you don't like anyone who's younger than you, that you're still mad about that 'queer's delight' crack. Just tell him the new people part.
jokes.setup: Larry wants Beverly to give Artie a cover story for why Cully is being let go.
jokes.punchline: Beverly escalates the list of reasons to a damning and accurate character indictment before Larry reins her back to 'just the new people part.'
jokes.explanation: Beverly's list is a great piece of escalation comedy — each item is more damning and more true than the last, while Larry's 'just tell him the new people part' is his desperate attempt to maintain the sanitized version of himself. The callback to 'queer's delight' is well-placed and shows Beverly has been keeping score.

jokes.text: Larry's uncomfortable around new people? What a crock of shit. As long as I've known Larry, he's been uncomfortable with new people. So fucking what?
jokes.setup: Cully has been told the cover story that Larry is 'uncomfortable around new people.'
jokes.punchline: Cully simultaneously calls it a crock of shit AND confirms it's true — he's indicting the lie as both false (as a reason to fire him) and accurate (as a Larry character trait). His 'so fucking what?' is the unexpected kicker.
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully constructed beat. Cully sees through the lie immediately, confirms it's essentially true, and then dismisses it as irrelevant — three separate logical moves in rapid succession. The 'so fucking what?' is the perfect button: he's not wrong.

jokes.text: It's not new people, it's me. He doesn't want me around. With me gone, he'll have you all to himself.
jokes.setup: Cully is working through why he's really being fired.
jokes.punchline: Cully's conclusion — that Larry is jealous of Cully's relationship with Artie — is hilariously paranoid and exactly wrong, yet not entirely without a grain of truth given Larry's possessiveness.
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Cully's theory: it's completely wrong (Larry wants him GONE) but also characteristically Larry-paranoid in its construction. The apple hasn't fallen far from the tree — Cully's as paranoid as Larry.

jokes.text: Oh, Christ, I hate this fucking near beer.
jokes.setup: Artie and Cully are having an emotionally charged conversation about Cully's firing.
jokes.punchline: Artie's sudden pivot to near-beer grievance in the middle of a heavy father-son moment is a perfect deflation — and tells us Artie is in some kind of sobriety program, a detail dropped without ceremony.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully timed deflation. Artie channels his emotional discomfort into a complaint about near-beer — the humor comes from the displacement, and the matter-of-fact delivery ('Christ, I hate this fucking near beer') makes it both funny and poignant. Very much an Artie move: he can't process the emotion directly, so he attacks the beverage.

jokes.text: Dad, don't fire me just because Larry's jealous. For once in your life, stand up to him. He'll respect you and so will I.
jokes.setup: Cully is urging Artie to stand up to Larry; the irony is that Cully caused almost all of his own problems.
jokes.punchline: The comedy is in Cully's complete lack of self-awareness — his impassioned speech about standing up to Larry ignores that he's the problem. And his invoking of 'respect' from someone who drove a Bentley into a bus shelter is absurd.
jokes.explanation: More cringe than laugh — the comedy is in Cully's blind spot, but the specific joke isn't as crisp as some of the surrounding material.

jokes.text: We have a wonderful show tonight. Mr. Larry King will be here. Good. Eli, those pants are a little snug. Will you take them out in the area?
jokes.setup: Larry is reviewing the evening's show plans, mixing in small talk.
jokes.punchline: Larry pivots from announcing Larry King as a guest to immediately critiquing Eli's pants — the banality of the costume note against the prestige guest name is the comic juxtaposition.
jokes.explanation: Light situational comedy. The mundane pants-note after the Larry King announcement is a nice deflation, but the joke is mild.

jokes.text: Why, because Cully hasn't learned how to kiss ass yet like everybody else around here? I just wanted my frozen yogurt frozen, that's all. Frozen it shall be, with sprinkles on it.
jokes.setup: Artie announces Cully is staying; Hank objects; Artie challenges him.
jokes.punchline: Hank's reduction of his entire grievance to 'I just wanted my frozen yogurt frozen' — stated with dignity — is both absurd and completely honest. Artie's 'frozen it shall be, with sprinkles on it' closes it with regal magnanimity.
jokes.explanation: A superb payoff on the yogurt running gag. 'I just wanted my frozen yogurt frozen' is a magnificent piece of Hank Kingsley writing — his complaint is simultaneously ridiculous and completely reasonable. The dignified delivery of this utterly petty grievance is perfectly in character. 'Frozen it shall be, with sprinkles on it' from Artie is a beautiful closure — regal, generous, absurd. This scores 8+ because it's a perfectly constructed payoff to a running gag with two great character-specific lines.

jokes.text: Who have you had on the show? We had president Clinton last week. Have you had him? Soon. Oh, we had Arafat, King Hussein, and Rabin, all together. No, we're an entertainment show here.
jokes.setup: Larry King and Larry Sanders compare guests — a professional measuring contest.
jokes.punchline: Larry King name-drops Arafat, King Hussein, and Rabin as a flex; Larry Sanders' response — 'we're an entertainment show here' — is a perfect piece of defensive self-deprecation that simultaneously admits the gap between their shows.
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry satire. The Arafat-Hussein-Rabin summit as a talk show flex is absurd and specific; Larry's defeated 'we're an entertainment show here' is both a self-deprecating laugh line and a genuine moment of insecurity. Captures the class anxiety of late-night hosts.

jokes.text: I can see this is a double Larry day.
jokes.setup: Both Larry Sanders and Larry King are in the same room.
jokes.punchline: 'Double Larry day' — Artie's coinage for having two Larrys to manage — is a breezy, economical throwaway that's funnier than it has any right to be.
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous economy. 'Double Larry day' is the kind of line that gets repeated — it's a perfect Artie coinage, world-weary and affectionate at once.

jokes.text: You know who you ought to have on? Brando. / I can't stop eating.
jokes.setup: Larry King is suggesting bookings to Larry Sanders.
jokes.punchline: Larry King suggests Brando and Artie immediately explains why that's impossible: 'I can't stop eating.' The implication is a Brando fat joke delivered via proxy — and Artie's deadpan causality is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy joke. Larry King suggests Brando; Artie simply says 'I can't stop eating' as if speaking for Brando. The joke is in the unexplained attribution — Artie doesn't say 'Brando can't stop eating,' he just delivers Brando's excuse. This compression is inspired. Gets funnier on rewatch when you parse the construction. Earns its score.

jokes.text: In the name of the sweet baby Jesus, why am I so fat? No, you're not fat at all. You're voluptuous. You have a great body. I'm fat. That's fat. Look at that. Yeah, that is fat, isn't it? Touch it. Just touch a little bit of that. Some of that's muscle, though.
jokes.setup: Larry King has apparently grabbed/presented some of his own flab.
jokes.punchline: The escalating negotiation over whether it's fat or muscle — climaxing in Larry King demanding someone 'touch it' — is a full cringe sequence. The comedy peaks at 'Yeah, that IS fat, isn't it?' from Larry Sanders, who briefly forgets to lie.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully uncomfortable scene. Larry King's 'In the name of the sweet baby Jesus' is a great comedy exclamation; the sycophancy loop (you're not fat/you're voluptuous) collapsing when Larry Sanders accidentally agrees ('Yeah, that IS fat') is the cringe peak. The visual of Larry King demanding people touch his body fat adds a dimension that the transcript alone can't fully capture.

jokes.text: Hey, Cully, were you able to get my magazines? The L.A. Times is on your table. Well, the L.A. Times is not a magazine. You see, Spin, People, Entertainment Weekly, those are magazines. Really? Thanks for telling me, because I wouldn't know what a magazine is. I'm a moron.
jokes.setup: Hank asked for magazines; Cully brought a newspaper.
jokes.punchline: Cully's response to Hank's condescending magazine tutorial is scorched-earth sarcasm — 'I'm a moron' delivered with no attempt to soften it. Then Hank doubles down.
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy: Hank's insufferable pedantry about the magazine/newspaper distinction earns Cully's brutally sarcastic takedown. The exchange perfectly captures why these two are incompatible.

jokes.text: Well, when you say the L.A. Times is a magazine, you sound like a moron. Get your own magazines. I'm not your errand boy. Look, I'm sorry that you're a 50-year-old P.A., but that's not really my fault.
jokes.setup: Cully has called himself a moron sarcastically; Hank agrees sincerely and then escalates.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm sorry that you're a 50-year-old P.A.' — Cully reframes Hank's position as the pitiful one, turning the power dynamic completely upside down.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines and the most vicious moment in the Hank-Cully dynamic. 'I'm sorry that you're a 50-year-old P.A.' lands because it's technically wrong (Hank is the co-host, not a P.A.) but emotionally and hierarchically devastating — Cully is treating Hank like the servant, and the insult reframes Hank's entire late-night career as errand work. The structure is perfect: Hank attacks Cully's intelligence, Cully attacks Hank's dignity. This earns 8+ because the line is specific, character-driven, and genuinely cutting.

jokes.text: Ow! Shit! Ow! What the hell was that?! Jesus!
jokes.setup: After Cully delivers his devastating '50-year-old P.A.' line, Hank apparently physically retaliates.
jokes.punchline: The sudden physical escalation — Hank apparently hitting or shoving Cully, followed by Hank's own injury — is a perfect slapstick reversal (the aggressor suffers).
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy beats rely entirely on the visual, which we can only infer from the transcript — Hank hurts himself retaliating against Cully. The slapstick reversal (attacker injured) is well-timed after the escalating verbal combat, and Hank's outrage at his own injury is perfect.

jokes.text: Hi, Cully. (Beat.) Shit. What? I had something going on with that one. Wasn't exclusive.
jokes.setup: In the immediate aftermath of the Hank physical altercation, a page (Betsy) greets Cully with apparent familiarity.
jokes.punchline: Cully's aside — 'I had something going on with that one. Wasn't exclusive.' — reveals a casual romantic history with a co-worker, delivered with zero shame immediately after a workplace brawl.
jokes.explanation: The casualness of 'Wasn't exclusive' — delivered as context, not apology — is the joke. Cully has managed to have a non-exclusive workplace relationship in what appears to be his first day. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Don't get involved with people you work with, no matter how sullen they are. Phil started it.
jokes.setup: Artie gives Cully advice about not getting involved with co-workers.
jokes.punchline: Cully's 'Phil started it' — a completely childlike deflection to blame-shifting — suggests the workplace romance is not between him and the page but involves a third party named Phil, adding unexpected complexity.
jokes.explanation: 'Phil started it' is a perfectly childish response to adult advice from your father — the regression to schoolyard blame is funny in the context of this grown man's brief disastrous career. Also raises questions about Phil that the episode wisely doesn't answer.

jokes.text: Don't you want to hear my side? No. Doesn't matter. Ha ha. You never want to hear my side since I'm 5 years old, right?
jokes.setup: Artie refuses to hear Cully's version of the Phil incident.
jokes.punchline: Cully's escalation — 'since I'm 5 years old' — suddenly makes this about their entire father-son history, taking a workplace argument into decades of parental grievance.
jokes.explanation: The shift from the immediate Phil dispute to childhood grievances is a well-executed tonal gear change — comedy sliding toward drama. Works as character comedy even as it sets up the more dramatic confrontation.

jokes.text: I broke the window, I stole the money that time. Yeah, I'm always the fuck up, right? ... Not after you stabbed the Great One with a fork! I was 6 years old. He was comin' at me.
jokes.setup: Cully lists his historical crimes to prove he's always been blamed.
jokes.punchline: Artie drops 'Not after you stabbed the Great One with a fork!' — Jackie Gleason, apparently — and Cully's defense ('He was comin' at me') makes the 6-year-old sound like he was acting in reasonable self-defense against Jackie Gleason.
jokes.explanation: The single best joke in the episode. 'You stabbed the Great One with a fork' is an absolutely inspired piece of comedy writing — unexpected, specific, historically grounded (Gleason was known as 'The Great One'), and wildly absurd. But Cully's defense — 'He was comin' at me' — is the perfect button: it's both childlike (blame deflection) and darkly logical (6-year-old self-defense). The image of a 6-year-old Cully being menaced by Jackie Gleason, then stabbing him with a fork, then being dragged off the Jackie Gleason Show set, is fully realized from a single exchange. This reaches 9 because it's the kind of detail that defines a character's entire history in one line, it's completely original, and it's deliriously quotable.

jokes.text: Parr, Gleason, Cavett, and now Larry. It's always the same.
jokes.setup: Cully has been listing his grievances about being blamed for things.
jokes.punchline: The list — Jack Paar, Jackie Gleason, Dick Cavett, Larry Sanders — implies Cully has managed to get himself fired from (or barred from) every major American talk show, spanning 40 years of television history.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy. 'Parr, Gleason, Cavett, and now Larry' implies an entire lifetime of talk-show disasters in four names. The absurd continuity — Cully has been a problem at EVERY significant American talk show — is both hilarious and poignant. The escalation from child (Gleason) to adult (Larry) suggests nothing has changed. Scores 8.5 because it's a masterclass in what you can do with a list: each name adds chronology, scale, and absurdity.

jokes.text: Larry, a guy who's so limp, he's like a fucking sock. Don't you dare call Larry a sock!
jokes.setup: Cully is attacking Larry's character to Artie; escalating the father-son argument.
jokes.punchline: Artie's furious 'Don't you dare call Larry a sock!' — defending Larry's honor against the specific charge of sockhood — is an absurdly specific piece of outrage. The image of a sock as a metaphor for weakness is funny; Artie's righteous indignation about the sock comparison is funnier.
jokes.explanation: A brilliant little exchange. 'So limp, he's like a fucking sock' is a vivid, original insult for passivity and weakness. But the joke's peak is Artie's 'Don't you dare call Larry a sock!' — the specificity of his indignation, that this particular metaphor is beyond the pale, is perfectly absurd. It's one of the most quotable moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Look at you! You're a fucking cheerleader for Larry! Larry! Larry! Larry! Hey!
jokes.setup: Artie has been defending Larry with escalating passion; Cully accuses him of being a cheerleader.
jokes.punchline: Cully literally cheerleads Artie's behavior — 'Larry! Larry! Larry!' — as a mock demonstration, which presumably involves physical movement that Artie then has to physically stop.
jokes.explanation: The cheerleader accusation is sharp — Artie IS a cheerleader for Larry, and the show knows it — and Cully's physical demonstration is a good escalation of the argument into absurdity.

jokes.text: Look at you! You're a fucking cheerleader for Larry! Larry! Larry! Larry! Hey!
jokes.setup: Artie has just defended Larry passionately.
jokes.punchline: Cully mock-cheerleading for Larry — 'Larry! Larry! Larry!' — while pointing at his father is a vivid physical comedy beat that encapsulates the whole dynamic.
jokes.explanation: The mock cheer is a good escalation beat. Physical and verbal at once. Slightly broad for Larry Sanders but works in context of the heightened argument.

jokes.text: You're fired! OK.
jokes.setup: After a massive emotional blowup about absent fatherhood and responsibility, Artie fires Cully.
jokes.punchline: Cully's 'OK' — accepting his firing with complete equanimity after everything — is the perfect button. The fight ends not with a door slam but with a quiet, resigned acceptance that punctures all the preceding drama.
jokes.explanation: One word after all that drama. 'OK' is the perfect anti-climax. The entire emotional edifice of the father-son argument — Artie's speech about responsibility, Cully's accusations — deflates into a single syllable. This is the Larry Sanders Show at its most precise: maximum comedy through minimum words. The economy score is 10 — you cannot say less and achieve more.

jokes.text: OK, this goes to Larry King, this to Valerie Harper, and the cactus goes to the comic.
jokes.setup: Immediately after being fired, Cully is still routing gift baskets — the physical comedy of him continuing to do his job post-firing.
jokes.punchline: 'The cactus goes to the comic' — an unexplained cactus for an unnamed comedian — is a throwaway detail that implies its own entire story.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the matter-of-fact continuation of work after being fired, and the specificity of 'the cactus goes to the comic' — we don't know why, which is funnier. Cully's complete emotional reset is a good character beat.

jokes.text: You know, you're being too hard on yourself. Horseshit. You're being too hard on yourself.
jokes.setup: Artie is beating himself up about being a terrible father; Larry tries to console him.
jokes.punchline: 'Horseshit' — Artie immediately rejecting Larry's consolation with a single word — followed by Larry repeating it anyway, is a perfect small exchange. Artie knows when he's being managed.
jokes.explanation: Great small moment — Artie's 'horseshit' is more honest than anything Larry can offer, and Larry's insistence on repeating his comfort despite being told it's horseshit reveals his own need to perform emotional support.

jokes.text: What the fuck do you know about kids?
jokes.setup: Larry tries to offer parenting wisdom to Artie.
jokes.punchline: Artie's blunt challenge — 'what the fuck do you know about kids?' — is simultaneously a genuine point and a dark joke about Larry's childlessness/selfishness.
jokes.explanation: A good puncturing beat. Larry's attempts at wisdom are undercut by the reality that he has no children and minimal empathy. Artie's challenge is both fair and funny.

jokes.text: Fine, I will have some kids of my own, but after the show.
jokes.setup: Artie tells Larry to mind his own business about parenting.
jokes.punchline: 'But after the show' — Larry's plan to have children is subordinated to his talk show schedule, with complete sincerity. His priorities are perfectly revealed.
jokes.explanation: One of the best Larry Sanders lines in the episode. 'I will have some kids of my own, but after the show' is a perfectly compressed piece of character comedy — Larry's talk show is so central to his existence that procreation is a scheduling issue. The casual 'but after the show' is devastating and deeply in character. This earns 8+ for character integration and economy: no other character on any other show could say this line.

jokes.text: Look at the bright side. Maybe he'll get that job at UPS that he wanted.
jokes.setup: Artie is worried about Cully after firing him.
jokes.punchline: Larry's reference to Cully's UPS ambitions — a callback to their earlier conversation — is both a genuine comfort attempt and a funny reminder that Cully's actual dream was a delivery job.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed callback that also functions as a genuine moment of Larry trying to be supportive. The UPS dream being invoked as actual comfort is funny because it's sincere — Larry isn't being sarcastic, and that makes it better.

jokes.text: Huh? What job? You didn't know that he wanted to get a job at UPS? That's all he talks about, Artie. No, shit. Yeah, he likes wearing the shorts, and evidently, they have trucks with no doors. I don't know. That's what Beverly tells me.
jokes.setup: Larry tells Artie about Cully's UPS dream; Artie didn't know.
jokes.punchline: Larry knows more about Artie's son's dreams than Artie does — and his source is Beverly, not any meaningful conversation. 'That's what Beverly tells me' as the source of paternal intelligence is a quietly devastating detail.
jokes.explanation: The emotional gut-punch of this episode: Artie doesn't know his son's dream job, but Larry's assistant does. The comedy and the sadness are perfectly fused. 'Cully always liked to wear shorts' as Artie's only contribution is both funny and heartbreaking.

jokes.text: Cully always liked to wear shorts. I don't get it.
jokes.setup: Larry explains Cully's UPS dream involves the shorts and open trucks; Artie processes this.
jokes.punchline: 'Cully always liked to wear shorts. I don't get it.' — Artie's father-memory is that Cully liked shorts, but he still can't connect that to the UPS ambition. The non-comprehension is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A small but perfect Artie line. He knows his son liked shorts, he knows UPS involves shorts, and yet the connection is beyond him. 'I don't get it' delivered after admitting the relevant fact is quietly absurd and perfectly in character.

jokes.text: I don't mean to be an asshole, but how long does it take to get vitamins in the mail?
jokes.setup: Larry is complaining about a delayed vitamin delivery.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't mean to be an asshole, but...' — a classic construction for absolutely meaning to be an asshole — about vitamins in the mail is a perfect Larry Sanders self-awareness-without-self-awareness beat.
jokes.explanation: A reliable construction ('I don't mean to be X, but...') deployed with good timing. Larry's self-awareness is always partial — he knows the phrase, not its implications.

jokes.text: Yeah. I saw them my first day on the job. I saw the package. I said, 'let me take this to Larry personally.' I spaced. I left it in the trunk of the car. Hope they're still potent.
jokes.setup: It's revealed that Cully had Larry's vitamins all along and forgot them in his car.
jokes.punchline: 'Hope they're still potent' — delivered with no trace of apology, as if the question of vitamin potency is a shared concern rather than his fault.
jokes.explanation: The callback on the vitamins is a good payoff — Cully has been sitting on them since day one. 'I spaced' with zero apology is perfect Cully. 'Hope they're still potent' as his only concern is a great button.

jokes.text: Hey, why don't we run down to La Brea to Pink's? We'll get a fatty with onions and sour kraut. I got a lot of packages to deliver. Aw, come on. Fuck it. I'll get to them later. Hey! Ha ha ha ha!
jokes.setup: Cully has returned — now in UPS uniform — and Artie invites him to lunch.
jokes.punchline: Cully's initial 'I got a lot of packages to deliver' (responsible) followed by immediate capitulation 'Fuck it. I'll get to them later' — abandoning his first day at his dream job for a hot dog — is a perfect ending for his character.
jokes.explanation: A beautiful character button. The brief flicker of responsibility ('I got a lot of packages') immediately extinguished by 'Fuck it' is Cully's entire character in miniature. He's going to be fine — and he's going to keep screwing up in exactly this way. The laugh at the end ('Hey! Ha ha ha!') is the sound of genuine reconciliation.

jokes.text: Isn't tampering with the mail a felony? Yeah, well, he's Artie's son.
jokes.setup: Cully and Artie go off to get hot dogs; Larry has just watched Cully abandon his mail route.
jokes.punchline: 'Isn't tampering with the mail a felony?' — a legitimate legal concern about someone abandoning a federal mail route — followed by Beverly's 'Yeah, well, he's Artie's son' as if nepotism is a legal defense.
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and one of its best. 'Isn't tampering with the mail a felony?' is a perfectly timed legal observation delivered with Larry's characteristic concern for his own exposure. Beverly's response — 'Yeah, well, he's Artie's son' — is both a callback to the nepotism theme of the entire episode AND a perfect encapsulation of how show business operates: blood ties override federal law. The structure is flawless as a closer. Scores 8+ because it's the ideal button on an episode about nepotism and loyalty, compressed into 12 words.

tmdb_overview: Family ties are stretched to the limit when Artie hires his delinquent son as a production assistant. Larry worries about his diet.
